dedupe_keys.name: agent based evaluation of dispatch policies for specialised emergency medical services vehicles and healthcare access equity

description: This case study evaluates rules for sending specialised ambulances, such as vehicles with advanced clinical capability, to different kinds of emergency incidents. Changle Song, David Matthew Levinson and Emily K. M. Moylan of the University of Sydney published it in Transport Policy in 2026. An agent-based simulation of a metropolitan emergency medical services system compares alternative dispatch policies under different proportions of specialised vehicles, tracking patient survival, response times and their spatial spread; the abstract does not name the study area. The article is available online, free to read under a Creative Commons Attribution licence. Caveats: the simulated system and incident data are not described in the abstract, and survival depends on the assumed clinical benefit of specialised care. Letting specialised vehicles attend a wider range of high-priority incidents raised overall survival, but when there are more specialised vehicles than demand, restrictive policies lengthened response times and worsened outcomes for other patients; moderately flexible policies balanced outcomes and equity, and disparities were larger in peripheral areas. The authors conclude that fleet mix and dispatch eligibility should follow the local mix of incidents. Simulation uses: policy scenarios and equity measures for ambulance dispatch and fleet composition models. Related records: the Region Zealand dispatch response time study (case_study-region-zealand-ambulance-dispatch-response-time-trends) and the Saint Petersburg dispatch simulation (case_study-saint-petersburg-ambulance-dispatch-game-theory-des) study dispatch elsewhere.
